propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA of a senior immigration officer's decision dated March 23, 2015.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] of a decision of a senior immigration officer [officer] of Citizenship and Immigration Canada, dated March 23, 2015, rejecting the application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations made by the applicant.

propositions.text: The officer rejected the applicant's application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
propositions.quote: rejecting the application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations made by the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of a senior immigration officer's March 23, 2015 decision rejecting the applicant's humanitarian and compassionate permanent residence application.

propositions.text: The applicant, Hanane Bouafia, is a 43-year-old Algerian citizen holding a multiple-entry visitor visa issued in 2012, expiring October 25, 2015.
propositions.quote: The applicant, Hanane Bouafia, is a 43-year old citizen of Algeria. She holds a multiple-entry visitor visa that was issued to her in 2012. The visa expires on October 25, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a 43-year-old Algerian citizen with a multiple-entry visitor visa expiring October 25, 2015.

propositions.text: The applicant's former husband and their three children are permanent residents of Canada.
propositions.quote: Her former husband, Hassene Belkhir (64 years old), and their three children, Ayman Rayan Belkhir (11 years old), Ahmed Laid Amastan Belkhir (9 years old) and Khadidja El-Batoul Belkhir (6 years old), are permanent residents of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant's former husband and their three children are permanent residents of Canada.

propositions.text: In June 2009, the applicant and former husband obtained a Selection Certificate in the investor class while married.
propositions.quote: In June 2009, when they were still married, the applicant and Mr. Belkhir obtained a Selection Certificate in the investor class.

propositions.text: After their October 2009 divorce, the applicant ceased benefiting from the immigration procedure where Mr. Belkhir was principal applicant.
propositions.quote: However, following their divorce in October 2009, the applicant ceased benefitting from the immigration procedure for which Mr. Belkhir was the principal applicant.

propositions.text: The applicant obtained custody of their three children as part of the divorce proceedings.
propositions.quote: As part of the divorce proceedings, the applicant obtained custody of their three children.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant and former husband obtained a Selection Certificate in June 2009; after their October 2009 divorce, she lost immigration benefits and obtained custody of the children.

propositions.text: On July 27, 2012, the former husband and two sons became permanent residents; the daughter became permanent resident on August 8, 2012.
propositions.quote: On July 27, 2012, Mr. Belkhir and his two sons became permanent residents; his daughter was granted permanent residence on August 8, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the former husband and two sons became permanent residents on July 27, 2012; the daughter on August 8, 2012.

propositions.text: The applicant currently lives with her former husband and children in Quebec and filed a humanitarian and compassionate permanent residence application on November 25, 2013.
propositions.quote: The applicant is currently living in the same residence as her former husband and their children in the province of Quebec. An application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds was filed by the applicant on November 25, 2013.

propositions.text: The applicant requested an exemption from the obligation to apply for permanent residence from outside Canada.
propositions.quote: In the application, the applicant requested an exemption from the obligation to apply for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds from outside Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant lives with her former husband and children in Quebec and requested an exemption to apply for permanent residence from outside Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant argues she wants to remain with her children, especially her six-year-old daughter, and that applying from outside Canada would harm the children and family bonds.
propositions.quote: In support of her request for an exemption from the obligation to apply for permanent residence from outside the country, the applicant submits that she wishes to remain with her children, particularly her six-year old daughter. In addition, given that she has legal custody of the children, if she were to have to file her application from outside the country, she would have to bring the children with her, thereby depriving them of the benefits of being permanent residents. Mr. Belkhir would also be deprived of his right to visit the children as a result of the geographical distance that would separate them. It is therefore in the best interests of the children to have access to both their father and mother.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues she should remain with her children and applying from outside Canada would harm the children and family bonds.

propositions.text: The officer refused the applicant's request for an exemption based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
propositions.quote: The officer refused the request for an exemption based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations.

propositions.text: This refusal decision is the subject of the judicial review.
propositions.quote: It is that decision which is the subject of this judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the officer refused the exemption request, and that decision is under judicial review.

propositions.text: The officer found the applicant did not establish that refusal of exemption would cause undue, undeserved or disproportionate hardship to her or significant impact on her children.
propositions.quote: The officer concluded that the applicant had not established that a refusal of the exemption would cause her to suffer any undue, undeserved or disproportionate hardship if she were to have to apply for a permanent resident visa from outside Canada. Nor would it have a significant impact on the applicant’s children.

paragraphs.summary: The officer found the applicant failed to prove refusal would cause undue hardship to her or significant impact on her children.

propositions.text: The officer found insufficient evidence that the multiple-entry visitor visa was not a viable option to remain in Canada during application.
propositions.quote: The officer noted that the applicant failed to provide enough evidence to show that the multiple-entry visitor’s visa she was granted would not be a viable option to remain in Canada and be reunited with her family while she applied for permanent resident status.

propositions.text: The officer found the applicant failed to show the hardship from applying outside Canada would be unusual, undeserved or disproportionate.
propositions.quote: In short, the officer found that the applicant had failed to provide sufficient evidence showing the type of hardship she would face if she were required to file her application for permanent residence from outside Canada and that such hardship would be unusual, undeserved or disproportionate.

propositions.text: The officer stated maintaining family bonds is not an exceptional hardship.
propositions.quote: The officer pointed out that maintaining family bonds is not of an exceptional nature.

paragraphs.summary: The officer found the applicant failed to prove the visitor visa was not viable or that applying outside Canada would cause exceptional hardship; family bonds are not exceptional hardship.

propositions.text: Issue: Did the officer err in assessing the impact of refusal to grant exemption on applicant and children?
propositions.quote: Did the officer err in his assessment of the impact on the applicant and children of a refusal to grant an exemption on humanitarian and compassionate grounds?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as whether the officer erred in assessing the impact of refusal on the applicant and children.

propositions.text: IRPA section 11(1) requires foreign nationals to apply for visa before entering Canada; officer may issue if requirements met.
propositions.quote: 11. (1) A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act.

propositions.text: IRPA section 25(1) allows Minister to grant permanent resident status or exemptions on humanitarian and compassionate grounds, considering best interests of affected child.
propositions.quote: 25. (1) Subject to subsection (1.2), the Minister must, on request of a foreign national in Canada who applies for permanent resident status and who is inadmissible — other than under section 34, 35 or 37 — or who does not meet the requirements of this Act, and may, on request of a foreign national outside Canada — other than a foreign national who is inadmissible under section 34, 35 or 37 — who applies for a permanent resident visa, examine the circumstances concerning the foreign national and may grant the foreign national permanent resident status or an exemption from any applicable criteria or obligations of this Act if the Minister is of the opinion that it is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations relating to the foreign national, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites IRPA sections 11(1) and 25(1) on visa application requirements and humanitarian and compassionate exemptions considering child's best interests.

propositions.text: Applicant argues officer's decision was unreasonable for failing to consider children's best interests and resulting hardship.
propositions.quote: The applicant, relying mainly on Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 [Baker], argues that the officer’s decision was unreasonable because he failed to take the best interests of the children into consideration. The officer neglected to consider that a refusal to grant the exemption under subsection 25(1) of the IRPA would create unusual and disproportionate hardship for the children in addition to having a harmful and irreversible impact on them.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the officer unreasonably failed to consider children's best interests and the hardship refusal would cause them.

propositions.text: Respondent argues officer's decision is reasonable, considering all evidence including applicant's multiple-entry visitor visa.
propositions.quote: For his part, the respondent argues that the officer’s decision is reasonable. The officer considered all of the evidence, including the fact that the applicant has a multiple-entry visitor’s visa in her possession. The applicant having failed to meet her burden of showing that her situation was an exceptional one that warranted the granting of an exemption, the officer’s decision was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the officer's decision was reasonable, considering all evidence including the applicant's visitor visa.

propositions.text: Officer's findings on humanitarian and compassionate grounds are reviewable on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: An officer’s findings with regard to humanitarian and compassionate grounds that deal with questions of fact and of fact and law are reviewable on a standard of reasonableness (Kanthasamy v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FCA 113 [Kanthasamy]; Azziz v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 850).

paragraphs.summary: The court states officer's findings on humanitarian and compassionate grounds are reviewed on a reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Subsection 25(1) IRPA allows exemption from applying outside Canada if justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
propositions.quote: Subsection 25(1) of the IRPA is an exception to subsection 11(1) of the IRPA and allows a foreign national to be granted an exemption from the requirement to apply for permanent residence from outside Canada if justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations.

propositions.text: Discretionary authority under subsection 25(1) is exceptional and requires proof of unusual, undeserved or disproportionate hardship.
propositions.quote: This Court has ruled on a number of occasions that this discretionary authority in an exceptional measure (Kanthasamy, above, at para 40; Lim v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 28 at para 20; Legault v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 FCA 125). An applicant seeking such an exemption must demonstrate that following the usual process provided for in the IRPA would cause unusual, undeserved or disproportionate hardship to them: [41] The Federal Court has repeatedly interpreted subsection 25(1) as requiring proof that the applicant will personally suffer unusual and undeserved, or disproportionate hardship arising from the application of what I have called the normal rule: see, e.g., Singh v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 11. The hardship must be something more than the usual consequences of leaving Canada and applying to immigrate through normal channels: Rizvi v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 2009 FC 463. (Kanthasamy, above, at para 41)

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 25(1) IRPA allows exemptions for humanitarian reasons requiring proof of unusual, undeserved or disproportionate hardship.

propositions.text: Officers must assign considerable weight to best interests of child but it is one factor among others in H&C decisions.
propositions.quote: When analyzing the best interests of the child, an officer must be alert, alive and sensitive to the best interests of the child and must assign considerable weight to this factor (Baker, above, at para 73). However, although an officer must examine this factor with great care, it remains but one factor among others: [A]n applicant is not entitled to an affirmative result on an H&C application simply because the best interests of a child favour that result. It will more often than not be in the best interests of the child to reside with his or her parents in Canada, but this is but one factor that must be weighed together with all other relevant factors. It is not for the courts to reweigh the factors considered by an H&C officer. [Emphasis added.] (Kisana v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FCA 189 at para 24)

paragraphs.summary: The court cites that officers must give considerable weight to child's best interests but it is only one factor among others in H&C decisions.

propositions.text: The officer carefully examined the best interests of the children and considered the applicant's multiple-entry visitor visa.
propositions.quote: In this case, it appears from the officer’s decision that he took considerable care in his examination of the best interests of the children and proceeded with a thorough analysis of the evidence adduced by the applicant. In particular, the officer considered the fact that the applicant had a multiple-entry visitor’s visa.

propositions.text: The applicant did not show any specific needs of the children requiring her ongoing presence in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Court also notes that the applicant did not cite any particular reason that would point to her children having any specific needs that would require their mother’s ongoing presence in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer carefully analyzed children's best interests and the applicant's visa; no specific needs requiring her presence were shown.

propositions.text: The officer assigned considerable weight to children's best interests but found no unusual, undeserved or disproportionate hardship from usual process.
propositions.quote: Thus, the officer assigned considerable weight to the best interests of the children but found, in taking into consideration the evidence in the record, that following the usual process would not cause any unusual, undeserved or disproportionate hardship.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer gave weight to children's best interests but found no exceptional hardship from applying outside Canada.

propositions.text: The court finds the officer's decision reasonable and dismisses the judicial review application.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out above, the Court finds that the officer’s decision was reasonable. Accordingly, the application for judicial review is dismissed.

propositions.text: There is no question of general importance to certify.
propositions.quote: There is no question of general importance to certify.

propositions.text: The applicant's eventual application for permanent residence outside Canada contains positive factors and antecedents.
propositions.quote: The application for permanent residence from outside Canada that will ultimately be filed by the applicant contains a number of positive antecedents and factors in the applicant’s favour, following several steps already taken by the applicant before federal and provincial authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer's decision reasonable, dismisses the review, and notes the applicant's future application has positive factors.
